summary:
VIGIL is our Earth system trend detective, built by a University of Plymouth team. It scans 25 years of NASA records, 2001 to 2025, across eight variables from air temperature to ocean chlorophyll. The planet is cut into 2.5° cells and every cell gets the same test, so nobody picks where to look. That came to 19,001 tests. Of those, 5,450 stayed significant after we corrected for running so many.

The challenge asks what is changing, where, by how much, and whether it is significant. Each trend answers all four: a cell on the globe, a slope with its 95% interval, and a p-value before and after correction. You can draw your own region and get its trends on the spot, or ask the AI Detective, which answers only from the findings. It runs as a Windows app and at https://keepvigil.earth.

Why it matters: VIGIL checks itself. Where a second NASA record exists, each trend is tested again on it, and the outcome is written on the finding even when the two disagree. Aqua MODIS confirmed 520 of our 632 vegetation trends. For soil moisture the two records disagreed on direction in 284 of 784 cells, and VIGIL says so.
details:
What it does and how it works

VIGIL is an Earth system trend detective. It takes twenty-five years of NASA records, from January 2001 to December 2025, and tests every 2.5° grid cell on the planet the same way to find where things are changing, by how much and how surely.

The scan covers eight variables: air temperature, precipitation, soil moisture, vegetation, snow cover, sea surface temperature, ocean chlorophyll and earthquakes. Seven are NASA products and the earthquakes come from the USGS catalogue. Each product is averaged onto one shared grid, month by month. Each cell's series has its seasonal cycle removed and is tested for a trend with Mann-Kendall, corrected for autocorrelation, with Sen's slope and a 95% interval for its size. Thousands of tests run at once will throw up false alarms, so the results go through Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate control. The scan ran 19,001 tests, and 5,450 were significant after that correction. It also looks for change points, for one variable trailing another in the same cell, and for neighbouring cells trending opposite ways, which brings the total to 6,122 findings.

The findings rank themselves, by a score whose weights are written in the run record, and the app opens on whatever came first. Each finding opens into its evidence: the series, the slope and its interval, the p-values before and after correction, the method, the source product and its limitations. Where a second NASA record of the same variable exists, VIGIL tests the trend again on it and writes the outcome on the finding, including when the second record disagrees. An AI Detective answers questions from the findings alone. It lists what it looked up, and this list can be interacted with, within the software and can take you to the exact grids that were cited for example.

VIGIL runs as a Windows desktop app and in a browser on desktop and mobile at https://keepvigil.earth. Both show the findings on a 3D globe. You can raise each cell by the size of its trend, play the years from 2001 to 2025, or draw any region and have its trends worked out on the spot. The globe also unrolls into a flat map.

Benefits and intended impact

Most tools for Earth data show you a place you already chose. VIGIL starts from the other end and tells you where to look, which is how it finds changes nobody asked about. Its top-ranked findings are the greening of China's Loess Plateau, which we never pointed it at. It also found a cluster of sudden steps in sea surface temperature in 2013. We distrusted them, checked them against a second record built from ships and buoys, and found they line up with the North Pacific marine heatwave known as "the Blob".

We want any user to be able to open VIGIL and get an honest lead: here is a change, here is how sure we are, and here is what the evidence cannot tell you. Every finding exports as CSV and GeoJSON for QGIS or a notebook, and links to its cell in NASA Worldview, so the lead can be followed up with other tools.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

- Desktop app: C# on .NET 8 with Windows Forms, including a software-rendered globe we wrote ourselves from NASA's Blue Marble and Black Marble imagery.

- Analysis service: Python 3.12 with FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, pymannkendall and ruptures. All the statistics live here.

- Data pipeline: earthaccess, netCDF4 and pyhdf, reading about 108 GB of NASA products through Earthdata.

- Web viewer: React 18 and TypeScript, built with Vite, using react-globe.gl and three.js.

- Hosting: an AWS S3 bucket for the site, AWS Lambda for the service, and GitHub Actions to build and deploy both.

- Hardware: one home PC did every download and the whole scan. The scan itself takes under four minutes.

- AI: Claude used to assistant with coding, ideation, research and troubleshooting (declared in the SI declarations). Utilised for the built-in assistant also.

How it is creative

The scan is the creative part. Nothing is chosen in advance, so the app can surprise the people who built it, and it did. Relief turns the size of a trend into height, so a fast-changing region stands up off the globe before you have read a legend. The Detective shows its working on the map: each lookup it made is drawn as the box it searched. In the C# application a presenter can press Present and have every phone in the room follow the finding on their screen, and anyone can stop following and explore alone. We intended to include this in the web application but sadly it didn't fit the scope due to time constraints.

What we considered

Mostly, how a tool like this could mislead, and how to stop it.

- Testing thousands of cells guarantees false alarms, so every p-value is corrected, and both versions are shown.

- A second record agreeing is not proof. Beside every confirmation rate, VIGIL prints how often the second record is significant where the scan found nothing.

- Soil moisture is the variable to trust least. Its two records are both models, and they disagree on direction in 284 of 784 cells. The app represents this.

- A region drawn by eye gives exploratory p-values, and VIGIL labels them that way.

- A lagged link between two variables is reported as an association, and not a cause.

- No statistic is computed or altered by a language model, and every result can be reproduced without one.

- We declare what was added after the first results had been seen: three variables and a stricter reading of vegetation.

- A link in a browser reaches more people than a Windows download, so the web viewer carries nearly everything the desktop app does and works on mobile.

The GitHub can be found here: Gurnski/VIGIL: NASA Hackathon Submission

Thank you for taking the time to assess our project.
- Daniel Rea, Ethan Jackson & William Ford
